title: Chest X-ray
what: A picture of your lungs and heart taken with X-rays. The radiation dose is small.
why: For cough, fever, shortness of breath, suspected pneumonia, or before surgery.
tell_doctor: If you are pregnant or could be pregnant
If you recently had an X-ray or CT scan. Bring the images

prepare.title: Preparation
prepare.text: No special prep needed. You can eat and drink.

prepare.title: Metal
prepare.text: Take off chains, pendants, and chest piercings. Tie up long hair.

prepare.title: Clothes
prepare.text: You will be asked to undress to the waist. Clothes without metal parts are easier.

steps: You undress to the waist and stand with your chest against the machine
You put your hands on your hips and roll your shoulders forward
When told, you breathe in and hold your breath for a few seconds
Sometimes a second picture is taken from the side
feel: Nothing. You do not feel the X-ray itself
after: You can go back to your day straight away
The report is usually ready the same day or the next day
red_flags: If it is very hard to breathe, your lips turn blue, or you have severe chest pain: do not wait for the X-ray. Call emergency services

faq.a: The dose is small, about the same as natural background radiation over a few days. If you need the X-ray, the benefit outweighs the risk.

faq.q: How is a chest X-ray different from a screening chest scan?
faq.a: A chest X-ray is clearer and is done when you have symptoms. A screening scan, called fluorography, is a quick check during a checkup.

faq.q: Why does the radiographer leave the room during an X-ray?
faq.a: Your X-ray lasts a fraction of a second, but the radiographer takes dozens of images a day. To avoid collecting a dose every time, they stand behind protection. For you, one such dose is small.
